beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 30 min cocktail hour, unattended, auto-advancing.

· Every other slide is the QR, alternating the two asks: BUILD (assemble) and ASK (signal).

· Check the radar is filling before you go on. If it is thin, work the room and point at the screen.

beats.label: OPENER

cue.prompt: Did you invent the words you’re using?

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 2 min. Fast. No throat-clearing, no bio, no app instructions — they have been on it for half an hour.

⚑ Do not answer the authorship question here. It returns in the last three minutes.

slides.text: Designed by systems.
slides.note:
→ "You were promised an evening about how the systems we move through shape behavior, decisions, and what gets built next."

→ "That’s exactly what this is — with one turn added: the loop runs both ways."

⏱ 20 seconds.

slides.text: Did you invent the words you’re using? Did you design the glyphs?
slides.note:
→ "Everyone’s arguing about whether you can tell if AI wrote something."

→ "But — did you invent the words you’re using? Did you design the glyphs? The grammar that strings them into sentences?"

→ "Or did you just put existing pieces together in your own way?"

⚑ Plant it. Do NOT answer it.

beats.label: CYBERNETICS

cue.prompt: The loop runs both ways. That’s the whole thesis.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 3 min. This is now the opening argument, not a mid-talk aside.

⚑ Astronautics, September 1960 — verified. Do not name Berlin or the pilot here; they have not happened yet.

slides.title: THE WORD THAT LEFT EARTH
beats: Cybernetic + organism. Not metaphor — a NASA engineering answer.
Don’t rebuild Earth in space. Modify the body to fit the vehicle.
slides.note:
→ "The word is younger than you’d think. Clynes and Kline, 1960, a paper called ‘Cyborgs and Space.’"

→ "It wasn’t a metaphor. It was an engineering answer to keeping a body alive somewhere it was never built to survive."

→ "Their answer wasn’t rebuild Earth in space. It was: modify the human to fit the vehicle’s loops."

slides.alt: 1964 Miami News cyborg diagram showing mechanical human modifications
slides.note:
→ "…functioning as an integrated homeostatic system unconsciously. That’s their definition."

→ "Unconsciously. If you keep noticing your prosthesis, integration has failed."

→ "Hold that word. In fifteen minutes you’ll be standing on it."

⚑ Quote exactly. Do NOT pair with any Spiekermann line — that beat is cut.

slides.text: The world shapes what you make. What you make becomes the world.
slides.note:
→ "That’s the title, and it’s the definition of cybernetics: feedback, both directions."

→ "That’s the claim. Everything after this is me showing you the receipts."

⚑ Rewritten for the new order — this is a promise, not a summary.

beats.label: TURING

cue.prompt: The test wasn’t crossed. It dissolved.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 2 min. Then walk straight into the radar with no gap.

⚑ "Nobody runs the test" is rhetorical — the Loebner Prize ran to 2019. If challenged, concede "no one treats it as the finish line" and move.

slides.text: For seventy years, this was the finish line.
slides.note:
→ "1950, Alan Turing. If you can’t tell — through text alone — whether you’re talking to a human or a machine, the machine can reasonably be said to think."

→ "For seventy years that faceless conversation was the finish line for machine intelligence."

⚑ Say the paper title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence.

slides.text: Nobody runs the test anymore.
slides.note:
→ "The veil wasn’t crossed. It dissolved."

→ "Ambiguity about human-versus-machine is now the default condition of any text you read."

→ "The frame that defined computation for decades just quietly went away."

⏱ Hold one beat. Walk into the radar.

beats.label: REVEAL
beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 3 min. The payoff for 30 minutes of lobby.

⚑ Never say "spectrum," "scale," or "where are you on the line." It is a shape, not a ranking.

slides.title: The shape of this room
slides.note:
→ "So if you can’t tell anymore — the only question left is who’s holding the bag. Park that. Look at this first."

→ "This is a radar, not a scale. There’s no far end, and nobody here is more cyborg than anyone else."

⏱ Point at actual spokes. Read the room’s real highs and lows off the screen.

slides.text: This room is full of cyborgs.
slides.note:
→ "You don’t need implants to be a cyborg. You built this over drinks."

→ "Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be. Diagnostic, not prescriptive."

· Plant "diagnostic." It pays off in the closer.

slides.text: Same area. Different shape.
slides.note:
→ "Two people can enclose exactly the same area and be completely different shapes."

→ "Vader is one shape — conspicuous, self-directed, obvious hardware. Ours is another: invisible and dispatched."

→ "Difference in kind, not a point on a line."

beats.label: THE PEOPLE’S SIDEWALKS
beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 4 min. The brief’s "resist and reshape" beat.

⚑ NOT "invented the curb cut" (Kalamazoo, 1940s). Say: first PLANNED wheelchair-accessible route in the United States, designed by disabled people.

⚑ Roberts LED the CIL, did not found it. Never name the dean.

slides.title: THE PEOPLE’S SIDEWALKS
beats: "We’ve tried cripples before, and they just don’t work out."
Berkeley builds curb ramps. The disabled community says: wrong.
They mapped 125 of them and drew the compromise themselves.
slides.note:
→ "Ed Roberts got polio at fourteen. Berkeley admitted him in 1962, and a dean’s recorded reaction was ‘we’ve tried cripples before, and they just don’t work out.’"

→ "More disabled students arrive. They name themselves the Rolling Quads and start using civil-rights language for something always framed as charity."

→ "1969, Berkeley puts in wide flat ramps. The response is not gratitude."

⚑ "a dean’s recorded reaction" — single-source, Williamson 2012. Never name him.

slides.text: The community was split against itself.
slides.note:
→ "Flat ramps erase the edge blind pedestrians navigate by. The diagonal angle pushes wheelchairs toward turning cars."

→ "Wheelchair users and blind pedestrians wanted opposite things. That’s the best detail in the story."

→ "1970 to ’74 they map 125 locations along Telegraph and Shattuck and propose a compromise they negotiated among themselves."

slides.text: The geometry was fought over. The texture was a gift.
slides.note:
→ "The ramp’s geometry was fought over in public by a community split against itself."

→ "The bumpy yellow texture has the opposite origin. Tenji paving — around 1965, one Japanese engineer, Seiichi Miyake, for one friend losing his sight."

→ "You’re standing on both at once — unconsciously. That’s the word."

⚑ Say "around 1965." Do not add a street name.

slides.alt: Curb cut with yellow tactile warning surface
slides.note:
→ "Sixteen years later the ADA makes it federal law. Today every stroller, suitcase and hand truck rides it."

→ "The system defined them as unable to move. They moved anyway, redrew the environment — and the redrawn environment redefined everyone else’s mobility."

→ "You didn’t design either one. And you move through both without a thought."

· This absorbs the cut bridge beat.

beats.label: RESPONSIBILITY

cue.prompt: For whose interests does the interface serve?

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 4 min. This beat alone now carries the accountability payoff — do not cut the stakeholder-table line.

⚑ Self-checkout is cut. Do not re-add it.

⚑ Soften the pilot’s bio if you are not clear to describe him: "decades in fast jets and then wide-bodies."

slides.title: REGENT / THE SEAGLIDER
beats: Brief: an interface for a captain who can fly.
Then the test pilot showed up. Call sign: Bob Dylan.
"That’s not where I expect it to be."
slides.note:
→ "Regent builds a ground-effect craft that skims above the water. The client defined the operator as a mariner. One wheel, one throttle."

→ "But the operational scope was aviation-grade and the mental model was maritime. That gap was the entire design problem."

⏱ Name the table out loud: me, biz dev, product, the CTO, program directors. All good people.

slides.text: He liked every concept. Every concept was wrong.
slides.note:
→ "Decades in fast jets and then wide-bodies. Tens of thousands of hours."

→ "Not messy, not unpolished — they didn’t match the logic his body had spent decades building. He’d tell me what he couldn’t see, not because it was missing but because it wasn’t where his body expected it."

→ "The real user changed, and the whole table reordered around him. We weren’t designing interface. We were translating fluency."

slides.text: For whose interests does the interface serve?
slides.note:
→ "To design responsibly is to name those actors, question their power, and decide how — and whether — they belong at the table."

→ "It’s one thing to make a beautiful interface in your tool of choice. It’s another to negotiate. Both land in the same place — the interface is where the negotiation gets painted."

→ "Send me your answer on SIGNAL now. We’re using them in the panel."

beats.label: RESOLUTION

cue.prompt: The question isn’t can-you-tell. It’s who’s accountable.

beats.presenterNotes: ⏱ 3 min. Close, then hand to the panel with the question still on screen.

slides.text: Not "can you tell." Who’s accountable.
slides.note:
→ "Once you can’t tell anymore, ‘can you tell’ stops being the interesting question."

→ "It becomes: who’s accountable? Who’s responsible for what gets said, decided, or made, when authorship can’t be resolved?"

→ "That’s why the pilot mattered. That was the table."

slides.text: Every word in your mouth was built by someone else.
slides.note:
→ "Did you invent the words, did you design the glyphs — no. You never did. And that was always fine."

→ "Some of it fought over, some of it a quiet gift from one person to another. None of it yours alone."

→ "Language was never pure individual authorship. AI didn’t break that. It just made it impossible to keep pretending otherwise."

· Keystone of the cut bridge beat. Must be said out loud.

→ "I’ve used the word cyborg to describe your practice for twenty minutes. That word is the intervention — language is cyborg technology."

→ "These are roles to borrow. ‘User’ fuses the person and the tool — what’s a user without something to use?"

→ "Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be. So — what’s the negotiation table you’re sitting at?"

⏱ Leave it up. Hand off.

beats.label: PANEL

cue.prompt: What's the negotiation table you're sitting at?

slides.text: What's the negotiation table you're sitting at?
slides.note:
→ "What's the negotiation table you're sitting at, in your own work?"

· Stage two or three and let the panel react to each. Don't lecture.
· Read it out, credit the handle. Let a panelist respond before I do.
· Second card. If two disagree, put them side by side out loud — that's the negotiation table made visible.

slides.text: In-house, agency, solo — whose interests are you suspended between?
slides.note:
→ "In-house designers sit between business interest and the interests of the person using the thing. Agency designers sit in that, plus agency profitability."

⏱ Hand this one to Justin deliberately. Peer dynamic, not hierarchy.
· Stage whatever comes back on the in-house/agency split.

slides.text: RIPTA is moving the bus hub out of Kennedy Plaza. Who was at that table?
slides.note:
→ "RIPTA's board voted in August to move the bus hub from Kennedy Plaza to the train station. Riders organized against it. The Kennedy Plaza Resilience Coalition has been fighting it since 2021."

→ "People in this room know this fight better than I do. So: who was at that table, and who wasn't?"

⚑ ASK, never assert. Do NOT state cost figures — they conflict (17M bond, 77M set aside, 200M estimates). Do NOT attribute motive to any named developer; that's reported opinion.
· Stage the sharpest RIPTA card. Let the room correct me — that's the point of asking.

slides.title: The room, revised
slides.note:
→ "Look at this against where we started."

⏱ If the shape has moved since the reveal, SAY SO. That's the room re-authoring itself in real time — best evidence I'll get all night.

slides.text: One sentence: what will you rename?
slides.note:
→ "Last one. One sentence — what word in your own practice will you rename?"

⏱ Three or four voices, fast. This is the language hack made personal.
· Stage the sharpest rename. Credit by name. Then let it land — don't add to it.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 25 min · facilitator, not expert · the feed IS the running order

· Stage cards, read them out, credit by handle

· Fallback if the feed goes thin: "what assumptions were embedded in 'a captain that can fly'?"
